paras: The threatened lynching of Ben Bethel took place at Pleasant Hill, in Talbot County, Georgia, on the evening of Sunday, August 5, 1888, when citizens assembled intending to lynch Bethel, a Black man accused of attempted burglary. According to the only report found, "cooler counsel prevailed" and Bethel was sent to jail at Talbotton.

Mrs. Sarah Brewster and her daughter, Miss Annie Brewster, lived alone at Pleasant Hill, and an earlier attempt to burglarize their house had been reported. The Savannah Morning News said that at midnight on Saturday, August 4, Annie Brewster awoke to find a man near her trunk who, when she made a noise, raised a knife over her and threatened to kill her. Her scream woke her mother in the next room, and the intruder jumped out of a window and escaped.

Bethel was captured on Sunday morning, and the paper asserted, without naming its source, that "evidence sufficient was gathered to fix the crime on him." That evening citizens, described as "very indignant" at the treatment of the "defenseless ladies," assembled at Pleasant Hill "determined to lynch the prisoner." The item gives no number for the crowd and names none of its members or any officer.
Instead of being lynched, Bethel was sent to the jail at Talbotton. No report of an indictment, trial or later outcome appears in the coverage found.

The episode appeared as one paragraph in a column of Georgia news in the Savannah Morning News of Friday, August 10, 1888, set among items on a hunting accident, a habeas corpus case and a veterans' reunion. The paper referred to Bethel as "a negro" and "the negro," treated the burglary accusation as settled, and presented the women as defenseless victims. It reported the plan to lynch Bethel and its abandonment without comment. No other white paper's account and no Black-press account was found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Ben Bethel
bases: Citizens assembled 'determined to lynch the prisoner' but were dissuaded and he was jailed, a threatened lynching with no violence reported (A1).

No one was killed: the assembled citizens were 'determined to lynch the prisoner, but cooler counsel prevailed' and he was sent to jail (A1). The episode is a threatened lynching prompted by a burglary accusation, not a completed one.
Only one paragraph in the Savannah Morning News reports the episode (A1); no second report was found.

accounts.label: Georgia news column (Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: A negro named Ben Bethel tried to burglarize the Brewster house, threatened Miss Annie Brewster with a knife and fled; captured the next morning, he faced an assembly of citizens determined to lynch him, but cooler counsel prevailed and he was jailed in Talbotton.

framing.detail: A short item in a column of Georgia news; it treats Bethel's guilt as fixed by 'evidence sufficient', stresses the 'defenseless ladies', and reports the lynching plan and its abandonment without comment.

Correct for the gathering (Sunday evening, August 5); the alleged burglary was Saturday night, August 4
